01 · Predict a reader's reaction

Warm-Up

A movie trailer ends just as a character opens a mysterious door. The audience cannot see what is inside until the next scene. That pause makes many people curious enough to keep watching.

Think like an audience member: A story can decide when readers learn important information, not just what information they learn.
Submit Warm-Up
Tank: A page break controls timing.
Forge: Reopen the file before you call it finished.
Joey: A clear ending lets the artwork breathe.
Percival.12: Credit the original author.
02 · A new published example

Group Learn — Sequence Is a Publishing Tool

Yesterday we studied how a single storybook illustration works with nearby text. Today we examine a different publishing decision: how a sequence of pages can show change over time.

In The Very Hungry Caterpillar, Eric Carle uses changing food illustrations, short repeated phrases and even holes in pages to make the caterpillar's progress visible. The reader experiences a sequence rather than seeing all the events at once.

New terms: sequence is the meaningful order of events; page turn controls when the next piece is revealed; continuity helps a reader recognize what stays the same as the story changes. A change of page can support the story's pace.

A publishing handoff also matters: Keep the original Google Slides document editable, confirm that the pages read in order and export the finished PDF if your class assignment requires one. The PDF is for reading; the Slides file remains the working original.

03 · Guided sequence challenge

Group Practice — The Bean That Grew

A science picture book follows a seed from planting to sprout to tall bean plant. The publisher has four small photographs and just three short sentences.

  1. Choose an order for the four images that helps a young reader see the change.
  2. Decide where one page turn would make the growth feel surprising or exciting. Explain that choice.
  3. Recommend a layout for the words so that none of the photos hides the explanation.
Look for more than decoration: a page's pictures, words and order can work together to show a process clearly.

05 · End-of-Part work

Perform — Mini-Quiz, Finish and Showcase

Resources for your storybook

📖 Read or hide the supplied story — Moss and the Rumor

At the edge of the foggy playground lived Moss, a shy green swamp monster. More than anything, Moss wanted someone to play with.

One morning, a crow whispered, “Moss scares anyone who comes near.” Soon the other creatures moved away whenever Moss walked past. Moss sat alone beside the empty swings.

Then a tiny hatchling wandered into the fog and could not find its family. Everyone heard its frightened chirps, but the mist hid the path.

Moss knew the swamp trails by heart. “Follow my footsteps,” Moss said gently. Step by step, Moss led the hatchling home.

The other creatures gathered around. “We believed a rumor instead of getting to know you,” one apologized. “Would you like to play?”

Moss smiled. The next morning, the swings were no longer empty.
